q: What is gross income?
r: All income received before any deductions
It is the starting point for figuring taxes.
w: Income after all taxes are paid
Gross income includes more than wages.
Tax owed is calculated from income.

q: What is taxable income?
r: Income that remains after deductions and exemptions
Tax is calculated on this amount.
w: All money a person has ever received
Taxable income is for a tax year.

q: What is a tax deduction?
r: An amount that reduces taxable income
It lowers the income that is taxed.
w: An amount that reduces tax directly
An extra penalty for late filing
A refund paid by a bank
A refund comes from the tax authority.

q: What is a tax credit?
r: An amount that reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar
Credits are more powerful than deductions of equal size.
w: An amount that reduces taxable income
A credit is not a loan.

q: What is a progressive tax?
r: A tax with higher rates for higher incomes
The rate increases as income rises.
w: A tax with one flat rate for everyone
A tax with lower rates for higher incomes
A tax paid only on purchases

q: What is a sales tax?
r: A tax charged on purchases of goods and services
The seller collects it and sends it to the government.
w: A tax on profits of corporations
That is a corporate income tax.

q: What is property tax based on?
r: The value of real estate or other property
Local governments often use it to fund schools.

q: What is withholding?
r: Taxes taken out of an employee's paycheck
The employer sends them to the government.
w: A bonus paid at year end
Pay kept by the employer as profit

q: What is the usual federal deadline for filing individual income tax returns?
r: April 15
If it falls on a weekend or holiday it moves to the next business day.
w: This is the start of the year.
This is not the usual deadline.
This is the end of the year.

q: Which form do most individuals use to file their federal income tax return?
r: Form 1040
It reports income, deductions and tax.
w: This reports wages from an employer.

q: What does the standard deduction do?
r: Lets a taxpayer reduce income by a fixed amount without listing expenses
It simplifies filing for most taxpayers.

q: When might a taxpayer itemize deductions rather than take the standard deduction?
r: When allowable expenses add up to more than the standard deduction
The larger deduction lowers tax more.
w: There would be nothing to itemize.
When they want to pay more tax
Taxpayers aim to pay what is owed.

q: Which of these is an example of an itemized deduction?
r: Mortgage interest on a home
Certain interest, taxes and gifts can be itemized.

q: What is an employer's role in income tax withholding?
r: Deduct taxes from pay and send them to the government
The employer holds the money for the employee.
w: Keep the taxes as company profit
Withheld taxes belong to the government.
Return the taxes to the employee each week
They are sent to the tax authority.
Pay the employee's taxes from company funds
The employee's taxes come from their pay.

q: Employees usually receive a refund when:
r: Their withholding was greater than their tax owed
They overpaid during the year.
w: Their withholding was less than their tax owed
They would then owe more tax.
They would owe nothing and have nothing withheld.
Filing late does not cause a refund.

q: What is a W-2 form?
r: A form showing wages paid and taxes withheld during the year
Employers send it to employees and the government.
w: A form to claim a refund
Refunds are claimed on the tax return.
A form to request an extension

q: Who is responsible for paying self-employment tax?
r: The self-employed person
They pay both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare.

q: Why do self-employed people often pay estimated taxes quarterly?
r: No employer withholds tax from their income
Payments are made during the year.

q: What is a capital gain?
r: Profit from selling an asset for more than its cost
It may be taxed at special rates.

q: Mia bought stock for $1,000 and sold it for $1,600. What is her capital gain?
What is the difference between a short-term and a long-term capital gain?
r: Long-term gains come from assets held more than one year
They usually receive lower tax rates.
w: Short-term gains come from assets held for ten years
Short-term means one year or less.
They are taxed, often at lower rates.

q: What is tax evasion?
r: Illegally avoiding paying taxes owed
It involves hiding income or lying.

q: What is tax avoidance?
r: Legally reducing tax by using allowed deductions and credits
It follows the law.

q: A business owner deducts a personal vacation as a business expense. This is most likely:
r: Improper and possibly illegal
Only ordinary and necessary business costs are deductible.

q: Which is an ordinary and necessary business expense?
r: Rent for a shop
It is common and helpful for the business.
w: A personal car for weekend trips

q: A sole proprietor has revenue of $120,000 and deductible business expenses of $78,000. What income is reported for tax before other adjustments?
r: Net business income is revenue minus deductible expenses.

q: What type of tax do corporations pay on their profits?
r: Corporate income tax
Corporations are taxed separately from owners.
w: This is a tax on specific goods.

q: What is double taxation?
r: Corporate profits taxed once at the company and again when paid as dividends
This applies to C corporations.
w: This is not the usual meaning.

q: In a partnership, how is business income usually taxed?
r: It passes through to the partners, who report it on their own returns
The partnership itself generally does not pay income tax.
w: The partnership pays tax and partners pay none
Only the oldest partner is taxed
It is not taxed at all
It is taxed at the partner level.

q: What is an S corporation?
r: A corporation whose profits pass through to owners' individual returns
It generally avoids double taxation.
w: A corporation owned only by the government
This is not what an S corporation is.
A corporation that pays no taxes ever
Owners still pay tax on their share.
A corporation based in another country

q: What is depreciation for tax purposes?
r: Deducting the cost of an asset over several years
It spreads the deduction over the asset's life.
w: Deducting the entire cost in the first year always
Some rules allow it, but depreciation spreads costs.
Adding the asset's cost to revenue
Selling the asset at a loss

q: What does MACRS stand for?
r: Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System
It is the depreciation system used for tax in the U.S.
w: Mandatory Accounting and Cost Reporting Schedule

q: Which statement about book depreciation and tax depreciation is true?
r: They can differ because the rules and goals differ
Tax rules often allow faster deductions.
w: Book depreciation is set by the IRS

q: What is a deferred tax liability?
r: Tax owed in the future because of timing differences
It arises when tax is paid later than book expense.
w: A refund due from the government

q: Which account records sales tax collected from customers?
r: Sales Tax Payable
The business owes it to the government.
w: The tax is not the business's revenue.
Collecting tax is not a business cost.

q: A shop sells goods for $400 with 7% sales tax. What is the total the customer pays?
r: $400 plus $28 of tax equals $428.

q: A business collected $1,260 in sales tax. How should it handle this money?
r: Send it to the tax authority by the due date
The business only collects it on the government's behalf.

q: What is payroll tax expense for an employer?
r: The employer's share of Social Security, Medicare and unemployment taxes
It is a business cost.
w: That is a liability, not an employer expense.

q: An employer has gross wages of $10,000 and matches FICA at 7.65%. What is the employer's FICA expense?
Which of these taxes is an excise tax?
r: A tax on each gallon of gasoline
Excise taxes apply to specific goods.
w: A tax on a corporation's profit
That is a corporate income tax.

q: What is the purpose of an extension of time to file?
r: To give more time to file a return but not to pay tax
Taxes owed are still due by the original deadline.
w: The return must still be filed.
Late payment can still bring penalties.

q: What is an IRS audit?
r: A review of a taxpayer's return and records to check accuracy
It confirms income and deductions.
w: A requirement to open a business

q: What should a taxpayer keep to support deductions in case of an audit?
r: Receipts and records
They prove the amounts claimed.
w: Only a written statement of totals
Nothing, because the IRS checks everything

q: A business buys equipment for $12,000 with a five-year life and no salvage value, using straight-line depreciation. What is the annual depreciation?
r: $12,000 divided by 5 equals $2,400.

q: Equipment cost $20,000, has a salvage value of $2,000 and a 6-year life. What is straight-line annual depreciation?
What is a tax loss carryforward?
r: Using a current loss to reduce taxable income in future years
It can lower later tax bills.
w: Moving the loss to another company
The loss stays with the taxpayer.

q: Which is a reason to keep personal and business expenses separate for tax purposes?
r: It makes deductions easier to prove
Clean records support correct tax filing.
w: It is not allowed by the IRS
It removes the need for receipts

q: What is a tax return?
r: A form filed with the tax authority reporting income and tax owed
It may also request a refund.
w: The return can lead to a refund.
It is not a bank document.
A list of the employer's costs

q: What is the main purpose of a Schedule C on an individual return?
r: Reporting profit or loss from a sole proprietorship
Self-employed people use it.
